nameStory: The Sandwich Tern gets its name from the town of Sandwich in Kent, England, where early ornithologists first studied and described this species. It's named after a place rather than food, though the shaggy black crest on its head does give it a somewhat disheveled appearance that might remind you of messy eating!
description: The Sandwich Tern is a medium-large seabird that's part of the tern family - those graceful coastal birds known for their spectacular diving abilities. It has a sleek white body with pale silvery-grey wings and back, and sports a distinctive shaggy black crest that makes it look perpetually windblown. These birds are roughly crow-sized and are built for life at sea, with long pointed wings perfect for soaring and diving after fish.

idTips.label: Shaggy Black Crest
idTips.description: Look for the messy, unkempt black feathers on top of the head that stick up like a punk rock hairdo - much more disheveled than other terns' neat caps

idTips.label: Yellow-Tipped Black Bill
idTips.description: The long, pointed bill is black with a bright yellow tip that looks like it was dipped in paint - quite distinctive among terns

idTips.label: Silvery-Grey Back
idTips.description: The upperparts have a pale, almost metallic silvery-grey color that catches the light beautifully, contrasting with the pure white underparts

idTips.label: Vocal Nature
idTips.description: Listen for loud, harsh calls that sound like 'kree-ik' or grating 'kerr-ick' notes - these birds are quite chatty and noisy

idTips.label: Plunge-Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for spectacular fishing dives where they fold their wings back and plummet headfirst into the water with a splash

habitat: In New England, Sandwich Terns are extremely rare visitors to coastal areas, particularly sandy beaches, rocky shores, and salt marshes. When they do appear, it's usually along the immediate coastline where they can fish in marine waters, often associating with other terns and gulls at productive fishing spots.

seasonality.spring: Exceptionally rare spring visitors may appear along the coast during migration, showing full breeding plumage with prominent black crests.
seasonality.summer: Any summer sightings would likely show birds in peak breeding condition with full shaggy crests and bright bill colors.
seasonality.fall: Fall migrants might show slightly reduced crest feathers and could include young birds with scalloped grey and blackish markings on their backs.
seasonality.winter: Winter birds would have white foreheads with reduced black crests, though winter sightings in New England would be extraordinarily rare.

funFact: Male Sandwich Terns court females by catching fish and presenting them as gifts - and the female will actually inspect the fish carefully before deciding whether the suitor is worthy, sometimes rejecting perfectly good fish if they're not impressed with the male's fishing skills!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the more common Royal Tern, but Royal Terns are noticeably larger and have orange bills rather than the Sandwich Tern's distinctive yellow-tipped black bill. Remember: 'Sandwich has a yellow mustard tip' to distinguish the bill colors.
contextualKnowledge: With only 9 recorded observations in New England, the Sandwich Tern is essentially a vagrant species here - most breed in Europe and winter much further south. Any sighting would be extremely noteworthy and should be carefully documented and reported to local birding communities.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Royal Tern, the Sandwich Tern is noticeably smaller and has that distinctive yellow-tipped black bill versus the Royal's all-orange bill. The Sandwich Tern's crest also tends to be more consistently shaggy and unkempt-looking, while Royal Terns can have neater, more swept-back crests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Royal Terns are much larger than their close relative the Sandwich Tern, with a bright orange bill instead of the Sandwich Tern's black bill with yellow tip.
